question: Is Pope Leo's prognosis 'excellent'?

sideA.label: Oncologists (pre-surgery)
sideA.text: Oncologists told AP that even if the nodule proved cancerous, the prognosis would be excellent because it was removed at an early stage.

sideB.label: Caution on missing data
sideB.text: The Vatican did not disclose the stage, whether the cancer spread, or what treatment may follow; a lung cancer expert quoted by the Detroit News said stage is critical to prognosis.

resolution: Unresolved — stage and follow-up treatment not disclosed by the Vatican as of Oct 13.

question: Was the nodule known to be cancerous before surgery?

sideA.label: Vatican bulletin
sideA.text: Preoperative tests suggested adenocarcinoma and intraoperative histology confirmed it.

sideB.label: Oct 11 announcement
sideB.text: Leo and the Vatican described a 'small, localized nodule' without saying it was believed malignant; the Vatican did not say whether cancer was suspected.

resolution: Disclosure sequence: nodule (Oct 11) then cancer (Oct 13). Vatican says suspicion existed pre-op; it was not stated publicly until after surgery.

question: Is the Vatican being transparent about the pope's health?

sideA.label: Vatican communications
sideA.text: The Vatican announced the nodule and surgery in advance, canceled audiences, and issued a same-day medical bulletin naming the diagnosis and procedure.

sideB.label: Observers
sideB.text: Theologian Candida Moss told CBS the Vatican 'tends to keep these things under wraps', so observers must read between the lines; stage and treatment plans were withheld.

question: Can Leo still make the Nov 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru?

sideA.label: Leo / Vatican
sideA.text: Leo said he planned to go, and the trip had not been cancelled as of Oct 13.

sideB.label: Medical timing
sideB.text: CBS reports air travel is typically avoided for about three weeks after this procedure, which would put the trip close to the recovery window.

question: Does the diagnosis affect Leo's ability to govern the Church?

sideA.label: Continuity view
sideA.text: Leo is 71, physically active (weekly tennis and swimming), and per Moss will likely keep working as much as possible, with cardinals and aides covering duties as needed.

sideB.label: Concern view
sideB.text: Cancer after lung-lobe removal raises questions about workload, travel and succession; the Vatican has not addressed these.

resolution: No official statement on capacity or succession; speculation unsupported by sourcing.
